description: Immortal Orbit (Antalya local event) is a one-person team: a youth participant supported by an adult advisor. I love games and space, so for the Space Mission Design Game challenge I built TUFAN, a 3D browser game where players design, launch and fly a planetary-defense mission to deflect a fictional asteroid. Every choice trades off mass, money, power and time. Play it: https://cemyurtlak.github.io/tufan/
summary: TUFAN is a 3D browser game for the Space Mission Design Game challenge. Players design a complete planetary-defense mission against a fictional 160 m asteroid: they choose a launcher, deflection method and rover instruments within a US$1 billion budget, launch the mission, drive a rover on the asteroid to measure its structure, then direct the impactor launch and steer it to impact. Every decision trades off mass, cost, power, data and time. The result screen explains why the mission succeeded or failed, so students learn engineering trade-offs by doing: decide, try, understand, redesign.
details:
WHAT IT DOES: TUFAN turns mission design into a playable chain of decisions. (1) Briefing: a fictional asteroid, "2026 TK7", may hit Earth in 10 years; it is 65% likely a rubble pile and 35% likely a monolith. (2) Design workshop: choose one of 4 launcher classes (capacity, cost, transfer time, arrival speed), deflection methods (kinetic impactor, anchored ion thruster, gravity tractor, or a combination) and rover modules (solar or RTG power, battery, spectrometer, seismometer, drill, antenna, fuel). Live gauges show mass, budget, timeline and predicted miss distance; an over-mass or over-budget design cannot launch. (3) Launch: the cinematic matches the chosen rocket. (4) Surface operations: drive the GEZGIN rover with WASD + mouse in low gravity (too fast and you exceed escape velocity), and step out on EVA to scan, place seismic sensors, drill cores, set the impact beacon and anchor the ion thruster. A day/night cycle switches off solar power, battery and oxygen must be managed, and data reaches Earth only during communication windows. (5) Launch base LC-39: as flight director, open the fuel valve, upload targeting data and run the GO/NO-GO poll; the countdown holds if wind exceeds 14 m/s. (6) Final approach: steer the impactor with RCS thrusters onto the beacon; aim accuracy sets momentum transfer efficiency. (7) Result: B-plane miss distance, delta-v breakdown, the asteroid's true structure, a score and a "What did we learn?" explanation. A presentation mode (F2) jumps to any chapter.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT: Students feel why real missions are compromises: a heavier instrument means a bigger rocket, a smaller budget or less fuel, and skipping a measurement changes the outcome. Failure is safe and informative, which invites redesign. It runs in any desktop browser with no install or login, in English (default) or Turkish.

SCIENCE: Simplified but grounded models. Kinetic impactor: dv = beta*m*v/M, where beta depends on interior structure (NASA DART measured beta of about 3.6). Ion thrust: a = F/M. Gravity tractor: a = G*m/d^2. Miss distance: dx = 3*dv*t. The asteroid's true structure is random each game and is revealed only by measurements. Asteroid gravity is scaled up for playability. The scenario is fictional, not a real threat.

TOOLS: JavaScript (ES modules), Three.js r160, WebGL post-processing, procedural 3D geometry, Web Audio synthesized sound, a small built-in language system (English/Turkish, switch on the main menu), GitHub Pages hosting. An offline single-file build is included. Source code: https://github.com/cemyurtlak/tufan

CREATIVITY: The player is engineer, rover driver, flight director and pilot in one mission, and only real measurements on the asteroid reveal which deflection strategy will work.

USE OF AI: The game's source code was written with an AI coding assistant (Anthropic Claude) following the team's design decisions, testing and feedback. AI also helped write the English README, the English translation of the interface, the demo slides and these submission texts. The game and the demo slides contain no AI-generated images, video or audio; demo screenshots are real gameplay.

NEXT STEPS: Accessibility, classroom testing with students, and cooperative missions where a team shares one budget. Learning outcomes have not yet been evaluated.
